column2: [The ministers said:] Suspecting a trick, they left these fruits and went another way; let this be known to you, king.
Thus told by those servants, Vrishadarbhi grew angry, and to repay them all he went home.
Going to the Ahavaniya fire and taking up a severe observance, the king offered one oblation at a time, refined with mantras.
From that fire rose a magical creature, terrifying to the world; Vrishadarbhi named her Yatudhani.
That creature, like the night of time, stood with joined palms and said to the king Vrishadarbhi, "What shall I do?"
[Vrishadarbhi said:] "Go, and hold in mind the names of the seven sages and of Arundhati, and of the husband's slave and slave-woman.
Knowing their names, destroy all of them; when they are destroyed, go as you wish where you please."
She said "So be it" and went, in her own form, to the forest where those great sages roamed.
Then they saw a very stout wandering mendicant with plump hands, feet, face and belly, a dog's friend, big-limbed.
Seeing him with all his limbs fattened, the fortunate Arundhati said to the sages, "You will be so; not so."
[Vasishtha said:] "For him the fire offering is not unoffered as for us; it must be offered morning and evening; so the dog's friend is fat."
[Atri said:] "For him strength is not struck by hunger as for us; what was studied with hardship is lost; so the dog's friend is fat."
[Vishvamitra said:] "For him there is not constant study of scripture, like an old cow, as for us; lazy, hunger-bent and foolish, therefore the dog's friend is fat."
[Jamadagni said:] "For him there is not food and fuel to think of for the year as for us; so the dog's friend is fat."
[Kashyapa said:] "For him there are not four brothers begging 'Give, give' as for us; so the dog's friend is fat."
[Bharadvaja said:] "For him there is not grief at a wife's blame, mindless kinsman of a brahmin, as for us; so the dog's friend is fat."
As they roamed once, they saw a lovely lotus pond covered with dense trees, with pure and clear water.
It was adorned with lotuses like the young sun in form, covered with lotus leaves like beryl in colour,
served by birds of many kinds that frequent masses of water, with one entrance, not to be taken, with good fords and without mud.
The magical creature sent by Vrishadarbhi, of terrible aspect, famed as Yatudhani, guarded that lotus pond.
Those great sages, with the dog's friend as helper, went to that lotus pond guarded by the creature, for lotus stalks.
Then, seeing that Yatudhani of terrible appearance standing at the bank of the lotus pond, the great sages said to the creature:
You stand alone; who are you, for whose sake, and for what purpose, resting at the bank of the lotus pond? Say what you wish to do.
[Yatudhani said:] "Whoever I am, I am; I am not to be questioned in any way; know, ascetics, that I am the guard of the lotus pond."
[The sages said:] "We are all afflicted by hunger and have nothing else; with your permission let us all take lotus stalks."
[Yatudhani said:] "On agreement you may take the stalks as you wish: each telling me his name, then take them without delay."
[Bhishma said:] Knowing that Yatudhani, the creature that wished to kill the sages, Atri, his mind possessed by hunger, then spoke:
Not-night is Atri's night, the night when one does not study three times today; Aratri Atri: know that as my name, fair one.
[The creature said:] "As this name you have told me, great sage, is hard to bear in mind; go, descend into the lotus pond."
[Vasishtha said:] "I am Vasishtha, the best, I dwell, I live even in houses; from being best and from dwelling, know me as Vasishtha."
[The creature said:] "This name with its derivation is spoken in painful syllables; it cannot be borne; go, descend into the lotus pond."
[Kashyapa said:] "Kula and kula, kupapa, kupayi, Kashyapa the twice-born, Kashya, from being bright like kasha: hold this as my name."
[The creature said:] "As this name you have told me, great sage, is hard to bear in mind; go, descend into the lotus pond."
[Bharadvaja said:] "I bear sons, I bear pupils, I bear gods, I bear the twice-born, I bear my wife without pretence; I am Bharadvaja, fair one."
[The creature said:] "This name with its derivation is spoken in painful syllables; it cannot be borne; go, descend into the lotus pond."
[Gautama said:] "Go-dama, damaga, adhuma, dama, durdarshana: know me, creature, as Gautama; Yatudhani, hear me."
[The creature said:] "As this name you have told me, great sage, it cannot be borne; go, descend into the lotus pond."
[Vishvamitra said:] "The Vishvedevas are my friends, and I am a friend of cows; known as Vishvamitra: hear me, Yatudhani."
[The creature said:] "This name with its derivation is spoken in painful syllables; it cannot be borne; go, descend into the lotus pond."
[Jamadagni said:] "Jajamadyajaja is a name, mrija, maha, jijayishe; I am famed as Jamadagni; so know me, fair one."
[The creature said:] "As this name you have told me, great sage, it cannot be borne; go, descend into the lotus pond."
[Arundhati said:] "I stay next after my husband, bearing earth, the sustainer, the bountiful; as one who follows my husband's mind, know me as Arundhati."
[The creature said:] "This name with its derivation is spoken in painful syllables; it cannot be borne; go, descend into the lotus pond."
[Ganda said:] "I have gone from cheek to cheek, called Ganda-ganda; like a cheek-cheek, know me as Ganda, in the flame's birth."
[The creature said:] "This name with its derivation is spoken in painful syllables; it cannot be borne; go, descend into the lotus pond."
[Pashusakha said:] "A friend to the friend who is to be friended, and always a friend of animals; know me as the secondary Pashusakha, born of fire."
[The creature said:] "This name with its derivation is spoken in painful syllables; it cannot be borne; go, descend into the lotus pond."
[The dog's friend said:] "As these have told their names, I am not able to tell mine; Yatudhani, hold me as the dog's friend, a friend."
[The creature said:] "The name you told me is unclear, spoken in a doubtful voice; therefore say once more now what your name is, twice-born."
I said the name once; since you did not take it, therefore, struck by a triple rod, go quickly to ash.
[Bhishma said:] Struck then on the head by that rod like Brahma's rod, the creature fell to the ground and went to ashes.
The dog's friend, having killed that mighty Yatudhani, planted the triple staff in the ground and sat on the grass.
Then all the sages took lotuses and stalks as they wished and rose up, glad.
Joined with great toil, they set the stalks in bundles on the bank, and made a water-offering from the lotus pond.
Then, rising from the water, they all came together, and they did not see those stalks, bull among men.
[The sages said:] "By what cruel sinful deed have the stalks of us, afflicted by hunger and wishing food, been taken?"
Suspecting one another, the best of the twice-born asked each other; they said, "We shall all swear an oath," scourge of foes.
Saying "Very well", all of them, hungry and exhausted, began the oath to the dog's friend.
[Atri said:] "May he touch a cow with his foot and urinate toward the sun, may he study on days not for study, who steals the stalks."
[Vasishtha said:] "May he be devoted to non-study in the world and drag dogs; may he be a mendicant by choice, who steals the stalks."
May he kill a refugee and a friend and live on his own daughter, may he long for wealth from a miser, who steals the stalks.
[Kashyapa said:] "May he sell everything everywhere, destroy a deposit, and give false witness, who steals the stalks."
May he eat meat in vain, give gifts in vain and go to a woman by day, who steals the stalks.
[Bharadvaja said:] "May he be cruel, having abandoned dharma toward women, kinsmen and cows, and may he conquer a brahmana, who steals the stalks."
May he put his teacher below him, study the Rik and Yajus verses, and sacrifice in a burning thicket, who steals the stalks.
[Jamadagni said:] "May he drop excrement in water, kill a milch cow and go to his wife out of season, who steals the stalks."
May he be hated, live on his wife, be far from his relatives and quarrelsome, and be a guest of one another, who steals the stalks.
[Gautama said:] "May he study the Vedas and give them up, throw away the three fires and sell Soma, who steals the stalks."
May a brahmana, husband of a shudra woman, in a village by a well-raft, go to his world, who steals the stalks.
[Vishvamitra said:] "May strangers support his teachers and servants while he lives; may he have no refuge and many sons, who steals the stalks."
May he be impure, a fraud in Brahman, and boast 'I was made by prosperity'; may he be a farmer and envious, who steals the stalks.
May he work for rain as a hireling and be a king's priest; may he be officiant for one not fit to sacrifice for, who steals the stalks.
[Arundhati said:] "May she always revile her mother-in-law and be ill-minded toward her husband; may she eat sweets alone, who steals the stalks."
May she in her relatives' house at the end of day eat barley meal, unfortunate and a bearer of no heroes, who steals the stalks.
[Ganda said:] "May she always speak untruth and quarrel with the good, and give a maiden for a price, who steals the stalks."
May she cook and herself eat first, live as a servant, and die by wrong deeds, who steals the stalks.
[Pashusakha said:] "May he be born only as a slave, childless and penniless, and not bow to gods, who steals the stalks."
May he give his daughter to an Adhvaryu or to a Chhandogya, though he is a celibate student; the brahmana who studies the Atharvan and bathes, who takes the stalks.
[The sages said:] "This oath you have made is dear to the twice-born; by you, dog's friend, the stalk-stealing has been done by all of us."
[The mendicant said:] "What was said by those who had done deeds without seeing the stolen thing placed first is true, not false; the stalk-stealing was done by me.
See these stalks, hidden by me here; this was done by me to test the blessed ones, sinless ones; and I have come for the protection of you all.
The Yatudhani, extremely angry, a magical creature wishing to kill you, was sent by Vrishadarbhi; she was killed by me, ascetics.
This wicked one born of fire would have killed you in return; therefore I have come; know me, brahmanas, as Vasava.
By your freedom from greed, imperishable worlds joined with all desires have been gained by you; rise from here quickly and gain them, twice-born."
[Bhishma said:] Then the great sages, pleased, said "So be it" to Purandara, and all went to the third heaven with the lord of the gods.
Thus these great souls, though offered enjoyments of many kinds, though joined with great hunger and tempted by great souls, did not show greed then, and so gained heaven.
Therefore in all states a man should avoid greed; this, king, is the highest dharma, famed as freedom from greed.
A man who recites this good conduct in assemblies becomes a sharer in happiness and does not meet hard places.
His ancestors, sages and gods are pleased, and after death the man becomes a sharer in fame, dharma and wealth.
[Bhishma said:] The theft done for the lotus long ago, best of the Bharatas, by royal sages, great king, and by twice-born sages as well.
The sages gathered at the western Prabhasa, assembled, consulted: "Let us all roam the earth with its holy fords; that is our task; come, let us all go."
Shukra, Angiras, and the wise Kavi, Agastya, Narada and Parvata, Bhrigu, Vasishtha, Kashyapa, Gautama, Vishvamitra and Jamadagni, king,
the sage Galava, Ashtaka, Bharadvaja, Arundhati, the Valakhilyas, Shibi, Dilipa, Nahusha, Ambarisha, King Yayati, Dhundhumara and Puru,
went, putting in front the greatly glorious Shatakratu, slayer of Vritra, lord of men; circling all the fords, they came to the holy ford Kaushiki in Madhya.
In all the fords, their sins shaken off, they then went to the very holy Brahmasara; plunging into the water at the god's ford, bright as fire, they were fruitful with eaten lotus stalks.
Some dug stalks there, king, others, the brahmanas, dug lotus fibres there; then they saw the lotus being carried off, which Agastya had lifted from the lake.
Agastya said to all those chief sages: "By whom was my well-grown lotus taken? I suspect you; let my lotus be given; you ought not to take the lotus."
[Kashyapa said:] "May he sell everything everywhere, be greedy about a deposit, and give false witness, who takes your lotus."
[Gautama said:] "May he live made by understanding and sell himself as the lowest; may he be a farmer and envious, who takes your lotus."
[Angiras said:] "May he be impure, a fraud in Brahman, and drag dogs, and be a maker of loss of Brahman, who takes your lotus."
[Dhundhumara said:] "May he be ungrateful to friends, be born of a shudra woman, and eat his prosperity alone, who takes your lotus."
[Puru said:] "May he practise medicine, nourish himself by his wife, and have his livelihood from his father-in-law, who takes your lotus."
[Dilipa said:] "May a brahmana, husband of a shudra woman, in a village by a well-raft, go to his world from greed, who takes your lotus."
[Shukra said:] "May he eat meat from the back, go to women by day and be a servant of the king, who takes your lotus."
[Jamadagni said:] "May he study on non-study days, feed a friend at the funeral rite and eat at a shudra's funeral rite, who takes your lotus."
[Shibi said:] "May he die without kindling the fire, make obstruction to sacrifice and quarrel with ascetics, who takes your lotus."
[Yayati said:] "May he beget in a vow-keeping wife, a matted-haired one, out of season, and reject the Vedas, who takes your lotus."
[Nahusha said:] "May a householder drive off a guest, may an initiated one be self-willed, and a hireling give learning, who takes your lotus."
[Ambarisha said:] "May he be cruel, having abandoned dharma toward women, kinsmen and cows, and abandon a brahmana, who takes your lotus."
[Narada said:] "May he be hidden and ignorant, speak out of tune to those who recite scripture outside, and scorn his elders, who takes your lotus."
[Nabhaga said:] "May he always speak untruth, quarrel with the good and give a maiden for a price, who takes your lotus."
[Kavi said:] "May he strike a cow with his foot, urinate toward the sun and abandon a refugee, who takes your lotus."
[Vishvamitra said:] "May he, as a hireling, make no rain, be king's priest and be an officiant for one not fit to sacrifice for, who takes your lotus."
[Parvata said:] "May he be an official in a village, go on a donkey cart and drag dogs for a livelihood, who takes your lotus."
[Bharadvaja said:] "The taking up of all sins toward the cruel and the false, may that sin always be his who takes your lotus."
[Ashtaka said:] "May he be a king of untrained understanding, self-willed and a doer of sin, and rule the earth by unrighteousness, who takes your lotus."
[Galava said:] "May he be priceless to the most sinful, a doer of his own sin, and proclaim a gift after giving it, who takes your lotus."
[Arundhati said:] "May she speak blame of her mother-in-law, be ill-minded toward her husband and eat sweets alone, who takes your lotus."
[Valakhilya said:] "May he stand at the village gate on one foot for a livelihood, a knower of dharma who has abandoned dharma, who takes your lotus."
[Pashusakha said:] "May that twice-born sleep in comfort disregarding the fire offering, may he be a mendicant by choice, who takes your lotus."
[Surabhi said:] "With the cord of balbaja grass for a fastener, may the milking vessel be bronze; may she be milked with a calf placed, who takes your lotus."
[Bhishma said:] Then, as those oaths were sworn, of many kinds, O lord of the Kauravas, the thousand-eyed king of the gods, greatly glad, looked at that angry chief of sages.
Then Maghavan, addressing that sage who had become angry, said his own conviction among Brahmarishis, divine sages and royal sages; hear that now, king.
[Shakra said:] "May he give his daughter to an Adhvaryu or to a Chhandogya, though a celibate student; the brahmana who studies the Atharvan and bathes, who takes the lotus."
May he study all the Vedas, be meritorious and righteous, and go to Brahma's abode, who takes your lotus.
[Agastya said:] "You have spoken a blessing, slayer of Bala, not an oath; let my lotus be given to me; this is eternal dharma."
[Indra said:] "Blessed one, I did not take the lotus out of greed; I took it wishing to hear your dharma; you ought not to be angry.
Dharma was heard, the elevation, a bridge of dharma free of ill, the sages', eternal, always imperishable; I have heard it.
So take this lotus, learned one, best of sages; blessed one, you ought to forgive my transgression, blameless one."
Thus addressed by Mahendra, the angry wise ascetic took the lotus, and the sage became pleased.
They went on again to the fords, roaming the forest, and bathed their limbs in the holy fords.
One who, composed, recites this account at each festival will not beget a foolish son and will not be outcast.
No calamity touches him, no fever or disease; free of dust, joined with good, he would gain heaven after death.
And whoever meditates on the treatise guarded by sages goes to Brahma's imperishable world, best of men.
[Yudhishthira said:] Not only in the funeral rite but in other meritorious acts too it is given; I wish to hear this at length and in truth, king.
[Bhishma said:] Hear attentively, king, the detail of the umbrella and sandals, how it became famed in the world and by whom it was set going.
And how it gained imperishability and holiness, and how it came: I shall tell all this fully, lord of men.
Hear this ancient event, lord of men: the conversation of Jamadagni and the great-souled Sun.
Long ago the blessed Bhargava himself played with a bow, setting arrows and shooting them.
Renuka brought all those arrows of his, shining with splendour, and gave them to him again and again, unfallen one.
Then, glad at the sound of the bowstring and the arrow, he shot, and she brought them back.
Then, when the sun had climbed to midday over the root of Jyeshtha, the twice-born, having struck her with arrows, said this to Renuka.
[Bhishma said:] He, stretching the divine bow and taking many arrows, stood facing the sun, in the direction the sun goes.
Then, as he was about to strike him, the Sun came up in the form of a brahmana and said, Kaunteya, "What offence has the sun done to you?
The sun, learned one, takes up with his rays the essence from here and there in the sky; and the sun rains that essence in the rains.
Then grain arises, brahmana, bringing comfort to men; grain is breath, as it is read in the Vedas.
Then, hidden in clouds and surrounded by rays, brahmana, he rains with rain on these seven islands.
Then from the herbs and creepers all that is produced of leaf and flower comes about by the rain, grain arises, lord.
All birth rites, vows and initiations, the cow-gifts, marriages and the prosperity of sacrifices,
sessions and gifts, unions and hoards of wealth go on from grain, as you know, Bhargava.
All lovely things and all undertakings arise from grain; I tell you what is known.
You know all this, brahmana, that I have told; I propitiate you, brahmana sage; why is the sun to be struck down?"
[Bhishma said:] Though entreated thus, the sage Jamadagni, bright as fire, did not at all become calm, descendant of the Kurus.
Then the Sun, in the form of a brahmana, with joined palms, bowed and said to him, lord of men, in sweet words:
The mark is moving, brahmana sage, since the sun is always going; how will you know the moving sun as he always goes?
[Jamadagni said:] "Steady or moving, I know you with the eye of knowledge; today I must surely impart discipline to you.
In the afternoon, Sun, you stand for half a wink; then I shall know you, Sun; there is no hesitation for me in this."
[The Sun said:] "Without doubt you will know me, brahmana sage, best of archers; but know that I am an offender who has taken refuge, blessed one."
[Bhishma said:] Then, laughing, the blessed Jamadagni said to him: "Sun, you need not fear; you are come bowing.
The honesty in brahmanas, the steadiness on earth, the gentleness of Soma and the depth of Varuna are in me."
[The Sun said:] "Great sage, take an umbrella to protect the head and ward off my rays, and leather sandals to protect the feet.
From today this will go about in the world and be the highest, imperishable one in all gifts of merit."
[Bhishma said:] Umbrella and sandals were set going here by the Sun; this is told as holy in the three worlds, Bharata.
Therefore give the best umbrella and sandals to brahmanas; great dharma will come to you; I have no doubt in this.
One who gives a white umbrella with a hundred ribs to a twice-born, bull of the Bharatas, prospers in happiness after death.
He lives in Shakra's world honoured by the twice-born, and constantly by apsarases and gods, bull of the Bharatas.
One who gives sandals to a burning brahmana, mighty-armed, to a bathed, sharp-vowed twice-born,
also gains worlds honoured by the gods and lives glad in the world of cows after death, Bharata.
This has been told by me to you in full, best of the Bharatas: the fruit of the gift of umbrella and sandals.
[Bhishma said:] Land that is fine to look at, wooded, adorned with coloured minerals and joined with all seeds is called best here.
I shall tell you in order the special field of it, the placing of tanks, and all waters.
I shall tell you the qualities of tanks and of those made; the owner of a tank is honoured everywhere in the three worlds.
Or a house of friends, friendly, increasing friends, producing fame, the best: the establishing of tanks.
The wise call the fruit of dharma, wealth and desire a well-made tank in a place, a field, a great refuge.
One should look upon a tank as for the four kinds of beings; all tanks give the highest prosperity.
Gods, men, gandharvas, ancestors, serpents and rakshasas, and unmoving beings resort to a reservoir.
Therefore I shall tell you the qualities remembered in a tank, and the fruit gained there as declared by sages.
He carries his whole family across in whose dug reservoir cows, and good men, always drink water.
One in whose tank thirsty cows, deer, birds and men drink water would gain the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
Whatever water they drink there, bathe in and rest by, all of it for the giver of the tank makes for endlessness after death.
Water is hard to get, dear one, especially in the next world; by giving drinking water, joy is everlasting.
Give sesame, give water, give lamps, be awake; rejoice with kinsmen; this is hard to get among the dead.
It is heavier than all gifts and distinguished above all gifts; therefore drinking water, tiger among men, is to be given.
Thus the highest fruit of tanks has been told; now I shall tell of planting trees.
Six kinds of unmoving beings are told: trees, shrubs, creepers, vines, bark-bearers and grasses.
These are the classes of trees, and these are the qualities in planting them: fame in the world of men and good fruit after death.
He gains a name in the world and is honoured by ancestors; even gone to the world of the gods, his name is not lost.
One who plants trees carries across both the past and future and the ancestral line, Bharata; therefore one should plant trees.
Those trees are his sons, without doubt; gone to the next world, he gains heaven and the imperishable worlds.
Trees honour the gods with flowers, the ancestors with fruits and guests with shade, dear one.
Kinnaras, serpents, rakshasas, gods, gandharvas, men and hosts of sages resort to trees.
Flowering and fruiting, they satisfy men here; trees carry the giver of a tree across hereafter like sons.
Therefore trees should be planted at a tank always by one who wishes the good, and protected like sons; they are remembered as his sons by dharma.
The maker of a tank, the planter of trees, and the twice-born who has performed sacrifices are honoured in heaven, as are others who speak truth.
Therefore one should make a tank and plant groves, sacrifice with various sacrifices and always speak truth.
[Bhishma said:] Here I shall tell you an ancient event, lord of men: the conversation of Vasudeva and the Earth, Bharata.
Having praised the goddess Earth, the mighty Vasudeva asked, bull of the Bharatas, what you ask me today.
[Vasudeva said:] "Relying on the householder's dharma, by me or one like me, what must be done surely, or having done what would one be happy?"
[The Earth said:] "Sages, ancestors, gods and men, Madhava, are to be worshipped and honoured; hear from me how.
One should always honour the gods with sacrifice, men with hospitality, and by choice as always those worthy always; by this the troops of sages are pleased, Madhusudana.
If he should question you, wishing to know of my approach, tell him of me too, fearless, as having mounted fire.
While you were away, a vast kingdom was kept by your son; for thirteen years varied wealth was enjoyed and given.
The mighty-armed old man, embracing Arjuna with his arms, weeping, remembering all his sons, lamented, greatly distraught, for his brothers, sons, grandsons, daughter's sons and friends.
[Vaishampayana said:] "All men, king, must go at the end of their deeds; hear this secret of the gods, bull of the Bharatas, which the greatly radiant, divine-sighted mighty one told."
